item.title: “Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
item.description:
“Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases; with the six sense-bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling … craving … clinging … existence … birth; aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.39
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then that monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, destroyed the hook, who has not fallen into misfortune, into calamity, not subject to the Evil One’s will. There are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then that monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, destroyed the hook, who has not fallen into misfortune, into calamity, not subject to the Evil One’s will.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.230

item.title: “Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle…
item.description:
“Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. What four? Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble virtue, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble concentration … noble wisdom … noble liberation, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is called a noble one.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is the burden? The five aggregates of clinging are the answer. What five? The form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging,…
item.description:
“Monks, what is the burden? The five aggregates of clinging are the answer. What five? The form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the formation aggregate of clinging, the consciousness aggregate of clinging. This, monks, is called the burden. And what, monks, is the bearer of the burden? The person — the venerable one of such a name and such a clan. This, monks, is called the bearer of the burden. And what, monks, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there — that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the taking up of the burden. And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance. This, monks, is called the laying down of the burden.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.22
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, monks, devas and humans dwell in suffering. They…
item.description:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, monks, devas and humans dwell in suffering. They delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … Monks, devas and humans delight in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, monks, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having directly known as they actually are the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in regard to form, does not delight in form, does not cherish form, is not excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, monks, the Tathāgata dwells at ease. He does not delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … Having directly known as they actually are the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in regard to phenomena, the Tathāgata does not delight in phenomena, does not cherish them, is not excited by them. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, the Tathāgata dwells at ease.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.136

item.title: “Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up badly; he has bad dreams; devas do not protect him; impure things flow out, nocturnal emission. These, monks, are the five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. Monks, there are these five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps well; he wakes up well; he has no bad dreams; devas protect him; impure things do not flow out. These, monks, are the five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.210

item.title: Elder Kappa: Full of various impurities, Where there is no purity — Like a long-stagnant puddle, A great boil, a wound. Full of blood and…
item.description:
Elder Kappa:

Full of various impurities,
Where there is no purity —
Like a long-stagnant puddle,
A great boil, a wound.

Full of blood and pus,
Sunk in a pit of filth —
This body oozes fluid,
Constantly oozing impurity.

Bound by sixty sinews,
Plastered with flesh as mortar,
Clad in skin as armor —
This foul body is useless.

Connected by a chain of bones,
Tied together with sinews —
By their combined power,
They create various postures.

Always heading toward death,
Approaching the end of life —
There, abandoned,
People go according to their desire.

The body, shrouded by ignorance,
Bound by four bonds,
Sinks in the flood,
Caught in the net of underlying tendencies —

Fettered by five hindrances,
Obsessed by thought,
Following the root of craving,
Covered by the veil of delusion.

Thus this body wanders,
Led by the chariot of kamma —
Sometimes success, sometimes failure —
Enduring many births of craving.

One who thinks ‘this body is mine’
Is a foolish worldling,
Increasing the fearful cemetery,
Clinging tightly to renewed existence.

One who avoids this body
As one avoids a snake smeared with feces —
That one abandons the root of existence
And attains Nibbāna, free from defilements.

From: Theragāthā 10.5
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “But here, Udāyi, a person thinks: ‘Attachment is the source of suffering.’ Having known this, he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment.…
item.description:
“But here, Udāyi, a person thinks: ‘Attachment is the source of suffering.’ Having known this, he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. Udāyi, I say: ‘This person is not bound, not fettered.’ Why is that? Udāyi, the difference in his faculties has been fully understood by me.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 66 – Laṭukikopamasutta

item.title: “Here, good sirs, greed is an unwholesome state, and ill-will is also an unwholesome state. There is a Middle Way that abandons greed and abandons…
item.description:
“Here, good sirs, greed is an unwholesome state, and ill-will is also an unwholesome state. There is a Middle Way that abandons greed and abandons ill-will, giving rise to (pure) vision, giving rise to (true) knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna. And what, good sirs, is that Middle Way that gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration. This, good sirs, is the Middle Way that gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 3 – Dhammadāyādasutta
